title: Cells and Body Systems
bigQuestion: If every living thing is built from cells, how do trillions of tiny cells become one working body?

story.title: The First Look Inside Life
story.kicker: A slice of cork, a drop of pond water, and two men who saw what nobody had seen before.
paragraphs: In 1665, in London, a scientist named Robert Hooke cut a very thin slice of cork with a sharp knife. Cork is the bark of a tree, the same stuff used to plug bottles. Hooke put the slice under a microscope he had built himself. The microscope had two lenses in a tube and a lamp to light the sample. He leaned in and looked.

The cork was not solid. It was full of tiny boxes, packed side by side like the rooms in a honeycomb. Hooke counted them. He worked out that a single cubic inch of cork held more than a billion of these little boxes. He needed a name for them. The small rooms where monks slept were called cells, so he called the boxes cells too. The name stuck. Hooke drew what he saw and printed it in a book called Micrographia.

A few years later, across the sea in the Netherlands, a cloth seller named Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground his own tiny glass lenses. His microscopes were smaller than Hooke's, but they were sharper. In the 1670s he looked at a drop of pond water, at rainwater, and at scrapings from his own teeth. He saw living things swimming. They spun, they darted, they bumped into each other. He called them animalcules, which means little animals.

Leeuwenhoek wrote letters to the Royal Society in London describing what he saw. Some scientists did not believe him. How could a whole world of living things fit in one drop of water? So the Society sent people to look through his lenses. They saw the animalcules too. A door had opened. Life had a hidden level, far too small for the eye, and it was everywhere.

It took almost two hundred more years for scientists to put the pieces together. Hooke's cork boxes were the empty walls of dead plant cells. Leeuwenhoek's animalcules were whole living things made of a single cell. By the 1850s, scientists agreed on a rule that still holds: every living thing is made of cells, and every cell comes from another cell. You are made of cells too, roughly 30 trillion of them, and they all started from one.
story.think: Leeuwenhoek's claims were not believed until other people looked for themselves. Why does science ask for that, and what would you have wanted to see before you believed him?

lessons.title: Every Living Thing Is Made of Cells
lessons.mainIdea: All living things are made of one or more cells, and every cell comes from an earlier cell.
reading: A puddle, a rock, and a leaf sit side by side in a parking lot. Only the leaf is alive. What makes it different? If you sliced the leaf thin and looked closely, you would see it is built from tiny units packed together. Each unit is a *cell*, the smallest piece of a living thing that is itself alive. The rock and the puddle have no cells at all.

This rule is called the *cell theory*. It has three parts. First, every living thing is made of cells. Second, the cell is the basic unit of life, meaning nothing smaller than a cell is alive on its own. Third, every cell comes from a cell that already existed. A scientist named Rudolf Virchow stated that last part in 1855. Cells do not appear out of nothing. They split.

The cell theory took a long time to build. Hooke saw cell walls in cork in 1665. Leeuwenhoek saw single-celled life in the 1670s. But it was not until 1838 and 1839 that two German scientists, Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann, argued that all plants and all animals are made of cells. They compared notes over dinner and realized their plant cells and animal cells were the same kind of thing.

Why does it matter? Because it tells you where to look when something goes wrong. A fever, a cut that heals, a plant that wilts: each of these is really a story about cells. If you understand how cells work, you understand how living things work.

words.d: the smallest unit of a living thing that is itself alive
the rule that all living things are made of cells, cells are the basic unit of life, and cells come from other cells

look.title: Virchow's Rule
look.text: Rudolf Virchow, a German doctor, summed up the third part of the cell theory in a short Latin phrase in 1855: omnis cellula e cellula. In English it means every cell comes from a cell. He was arguing against the older idea that cells could form on their own out of fluid, the way crystals form.
look.cite: Rudolf Virchow, lecture and essay on cellular pathology, 1855
look.prompt: If every cell comes from a cell, where did the very first cell in your body come from?

check.q: Which of these is made of cells?
check.why: Only living things are made of cells. The dandelion is alive; the others are not.

check.q: What does the cell theory say about where new cells come from?
choices: They form out of thin air
They come from cells that already exist
They are made by the brain
check.why: Virchow's rule states that every cell comes from an earlier cell, which splits.

check.q: Why did it take so long to build the cell theory after Hooke saw cork in 1665?
choices: Scientists had to look at many plants and animals and compare them
check.why: Schleiden and Schwann had to study many samples before arguing that all plants and animals share the same building block.

lessons.title: Through the Microscope
lessons.mainIdea: A microscope bends light through lenses to make tiny things look large enough to study.
reading: Your eye can see a grain of salt, but not the cells in your own skin. Most cells are far too small. A typical animal cell is about one fiftieth of a millimeter across. To see one, you need a tool that makes small things look bigger. That tool is a *microscope*. It works by bending light through curved pieces of glass called lenses.

In a light microscope, light shines up through a thin sample. A lens near the sample bends the light so the image spreads out. A second lens in the eyepiece spreads it out again. Together they *magnify* the image. If the first lens magnifies 40 times and the second 10 times, you see the sample 400 times larger than life. That is enough to see most cells clearly.

The site's own microscope works this way. When you place a slice of onion skin on the stage and turn the focus knob, the blur snaps into a grid of boxes. Those are cells, each with a small dark dot near the middle. Leeuwenhoek's microscope was simpler, with just one tiny bead of glass, but he ground it so well it could magnify more than 200 times.

Light microscopes have a limit. Light itself has a size, a wavelength, and details smaller than that blur together. To see the inside of a cell in fine detail, scientists built the electron microscope in the 1930s. It uses a beam of electrons instead of light and can magnify hundreds of thousands of times.

words.d: a tool that uses lenses to make very small things look large
to make something appear larger than it really is

look.title: How Big Are Cells?
look.prompt: A human hair is about 80 micrometers wide. Which of these cells could you line up ten across on a single hair?

check.q: What does a lens do to light in a microscope?
choices: Bends it so the image spreads out
check.why: Curved glass bends light, spreading the image so it looks larger.

check.q: A microscope has a 4x lens and a 10x eyepiece. How much bigger does the sample look?
check.why: The two lenses multiply: 4 times 10 is 40.

check.q: Why did scientists build the electron microscope?
choices: Light cannot show details smaller than its own wavelength
check.why: Light has a wavelength, and details smaller than that blur together. Electrons can show much finer detail.

lessons.title: One Cell or Many
lessons.mainIdea: Some living things are a single cell that does everything; others are many cells that share the work.
reading: Scoop a jar of water from a pond in a Chicago park and let it sit in the light. Within a day it is a city. Under the microscope you will see round green cells, oval cells covered in beating hairs, and blobs that flow along and change shape. Each one is a whole living thing made of one cell. We call them *unicellular*, from the Latin for one cell.

A unicellular organism has to do every job of life inside one cell. It takes in food, gets rid of waste, senses its surroundings, and splits to make more of itself. Bacteria are unicellular. So are the amoeba and the paramecium in your pond jar. Yeast, the tiny fungus that makes bread rise, is unicellular too.

You are *multicellular*. So is a maple tree, a mushroom, and a mosquito. In a multicellular organism, cells share the work. Some cells carry oxygen. Some send signals. Some make bone. No single cell in your body could live on its own for long, but together they make one organism that can run, think, and grow.

Both ways of living work. Unicellular life has been on Earth for more than three billion years and is still everywhere, in soil, sea, and your own gut. Multicellular life came later, and it made possible things a single cell cannot do, such as growing large or moving fast. Neither is better. They are two answers to the same problem: how to stay alive.

words.d: made of only one cell
made of many cells that share the work of staying alive
any single living thing, whether one cell or trillions

look.title: Little Animals in a Drop
look.text: In a letter to the Royal Society in 1676, Leeuwenhoek described water in which he had soaked pepper. He wrote that he found an incredible number of very small living creatures moving about in it, so small that he judged that many thousands of them together would not equal the size of a grain of coarse sand.
look.cite: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, letter to the Royal Society of London, October 1676
look.prompt: Leeuwenhoek compared the creatures to a grain of sand. Why is comparing to a familiar object a useful way to describe a size?

check.q: Which of these is unicellular?
check.why: A bacterium is a single cell. The others are made of many cells.

check.q: What must a unicellular organism do that a single cell in your body does not have to do?
choices: Do every job of life by itself
check.why: Cells in your body share jobs. A unicellular organism has no other cells to help.

check.q: Which statement about unicellular and multicellular life is true?
choices: Both are still common on Earth today
Unicellular life died out long ago
check.why: Unicellular life is still everywhere, and it came before multicellular life. Both are alive.

lessons.title: The Membrane and the Nucleus
lessons.mainIdea: The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves, and the nucleus holds the instructions.
reading: Picture a cell as a tiny factory. A factory needs walls with doors, and it needs an office that keeps the plans. In a cell, the wall with doors is the *cell membrane*. It is a thin, flexible layer that wraps the whole cell. It is not a solid bag. It lets some things through and keeps others out. Water and oxygen slip in. Waste is pushed out. Larger things need a special gate.

Inside the membrane is a jelly-like fluid called *cytoplasm*. Most of the cell's work happens here. Floating in the cytoplasm are small structures with different jobs. Scientists call them *organelles*, which means little organs. Each organelle does one kind of task, just as each machine in a factory does one kind of task.

The largest organelle in most animal and plant cells is the *nucleus*. That is the small dark dot you saw in the onion skin. The nucleus holds the cell's instructions, written in a long molecule called DNA. Those instructions tell the cell what proteins to build. When a cell divides, it first copies the DNA so each new cell gets a full set.

Not every cell has a nucleus. Bacteria do not. Their DNA floats loose in the cytoplasm. Scientists split all life into two groups on exactly this point. Cells with a nucleus are called eukaryotic, and cells without one are prokaryotic. Every plant, animal, and fungus is eukaryotic. Bacteria are prokaryotic.

words.d: the thin outer layer of a cell that controls what goes in and out
the jelly-like fluid inside a cell where most of its work happens
small structures inside a cell, each with its own job
the organelle that holds a cell's DNA instructions

look.title: A Bag That Chooses
look.text: Fill a plastic bag with water and tie it shut. Nothing gets in or out. Now imagine a bag with millions of tiny doors, each shaped to let only one kind of thing pass. Water can slip through gaps. Sugar needs a door that opens for sugar. Waste has its own door going out. That is closer to what a cell membrane is.
look.prompt: What would happen to a cell if its membrane let everything through, with no doors at all?

check.q: What is the job of the cell membrane?
choices: To control what enters and leaves the cell
check.why: The membrane wraps the cell and lets some things through while keeping others out.

check.q: Where are a cell's DNA instructions kept in a plant or animal cell?
check.why: The nucleus holds the DNA in eukaryotic cells such as plant and animal cells.

check.q: A cell has no nucleus, and its DNA floats loose. What kind of cell is it most likely?
check.why: Bacteria are prokaryotic, meaning they have no nucleus.

lessons.title: Mitochondria: Where Fuel Becomes Energy
lessons.mainIdea: Mitochondria break down food using oxygen to release energy the cell can use.
reading: You eat a sandwich, and an hour later you run up the stairs. Somewhere in between, food turned into motion. That change happens inside organelles called *mitochondria*. A mitochondrion is a small bean-shaped structure with a folded inner layer. Nearly every cell in your body has them, from a few dozen to thousands.

Inside a mitochondrion, sugar from food is broken apart step by step with the help of oxygen. Each step releases a little energy. The cell catches that energy in a small molecule called ATP and uses it to power everything else: building proteins, moving, sending signals. This whole process is called *cellular respiration*, and it is why you breathe. The oxygen you take in goes to your mitochondria.

Cells that work hard have more mitochondria. A muscle cell in your leg is packed with them. A heart cell, which never rests, has even more. A skin cell has fewer. If you look at where the mitochondria are, you can guess what the cell does.

Mitochondria also have a strange history. They carry their own small loop of DNA, separate from the nucleus. Scientists think that long ago they were free-living bacteria that were taken inside a larger cell and stayed. The bacterium got a safe home. The larger cell got a power supply. That partnership is inside every cell of your body.

words.d: organelles that break down food with oxygen to release energy for the cell
the process in which cells break down sugar with oxygen to release energy

look.title: Two Cells, Two Jobs
look.text: Under the microscope, two cells from the same person sit side by side. One came from the heart. It is crammed with hundreds of bean-shaped mitochondria. The other came from the outer layer of the skin. It has only a few. Both cells have the same DNA and the same membrane.
look.prompt: Why would a heart cell need so many more mitochondria than a skin cell? What does that tell you about how the body spends energy?

check.q: What do mitochondria do?
check.why: Mitochondria break down sugar with oxygen and release energy for the cell.

check.q: Which cell would you expect to have the most mitochondria?
check.why: Cells that work hard all the time, like heart cells, need many mitochondria.

check.q: Why do you need to breathe in oxygen?
choices: Oxygen makes blood red so it can move
Mitochondria use oxygen to release energy from food
check.why: Cellular respiration in the mitochondria needs oxygen to break sugar down and release energy.

lessons.title: Plant Cells: Chloroplasts and Walls
lessons.mainIdea: Plant cells have chloroplasts that capture light and a stiff cell wall that gives them shape.
reading: Put a leaf and a slice of your cheek under the same microscope. Both show cells with a membrane, cytoplasm, and a nucleus. But the leaf cells have two things your cheek cells lack. They are green, and they are boxy. Those two differences explain a lot about how a plant lives.

The green comes from organelles called *chloroplasts*. Each one is filled with a green substance called chlorophyll that catches light. Inside the chloroplast, the plant uses that light energy to build sugar out of carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil. This is *photosynthesis*. It is how a plant makes its own food. Animals cannot do it, so they must eat.

The boxy shape comes from the *cell wall*, a stiff layer outside the membrane. It is made mostly of a tough fiber called cellulose. The wall holds the cell in shape and lets a plant stand up without bones. When Hooke saw cork, he was seeing cell walls left behind after the cells inside had died. Plant cells also have a large water-filled sac called a vacuole. When the vacuole is full, the cell is firm. When it empties, the plant wilts.

So a plant cell is a factory with its own solar panel and its own concrete walls. An animal cell has neither. It gets its energy by eating and its shape from the cells around it. Both kinds of cell keep their instructions in a nucleus and release energy in mitochondria. The differences are about how they get food and how they hold their shape.

words.d: green organelles in plant cells that capture light energy to make sugar
the process in which plants use light, water, and carbon dioxide to make sugar and oxygen
a stiff outer layer around plant cells that gives them shape and support

look.title: Hooke's Honeycomb
look.text: In Micrographia, Hooke described the thin slice of cork he saw through his microscope. He wrote that he could see very plainly that it was all full of holes and pores, much like a honeycomb, though the pores were not regular. He then estimated that a cubic inch of cork contained more than a billion of these little cells.
look.prompt: Hooke was looking at cork, which is dead bark. Which part of a plant cell was he actually seeing, and why was it still there?

check.q: What makes a plant cell green?
check.why: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, the green substance that captures light.

check.q: Which structure gives a plant cell its boxy shape and lets a plant stand up without bones?
check.why: The stiff cell wall outside the membrane holds each cell in shape.

check.q: Which of these do plant cells and animal cells share?
choices: The ability to make their own food
check.why: Both kinds of cell have a nucleus and mitochondria. Only plant cells have walls and chloroplasts.

lessons.title: Cells, Tissues, Organs, Systems
lessons.mainIdea: Cells group into tissues, tissues build organs, and organs work together as systems.
reading: A brick alone is not a house. A cell alone is not a body. To build something big, living things stack cells in levels. Each level is made of the one below it and does something the lower level cannot do by itself. Learning the levels gives you a map of any animal or plant.

The first level up from the cell is the *tissue*. A tissue is a group of similar cells doing the same job. Muscle tissue is made of cells that shorten. Nerve tissue is made of cells that carry signals. Your skin has a tissue that covers and protects. Your body has four main kinds of tissue: muscle, nerve, connective, and covering.

Tissues combine to make an *organ*. Your heart is an organ. It has muscle tissue to squeeze, nerve tissue to set the beat, and connective tissue to hold it together. Your stomach, lungs, brain, and skin are organs too. A leaf is a plant organ, and so is a root.

Organs that work toward one goal make up an *organ system*. The mouth, stomach, and intestines form the digestive system. The heart and blood vessels form the circulatory system. Your body has about a dozen systems, and none works alone. Cells, tissues, organs, systems, organism: that is the ladder from the smallest living unit to you.

words.d: a group of similar cells that work together on one job
a body part made of several tissues that does a specific job, such as the heart or a leaf
a group of organs that work together toward one goal, such as digesting food

look.title: Zooming Out From One Cell
look.text: Start with a single muscle cell in your upper arm, a long thin fiber that can shorten. Zoom out: thousands of these fibers lie side by side in a bundle, all pulling the same way. Zoom out again: the bundle is the biceps, wrapped in connective tissue and wired with nerves. Zoom out once more: the biceps, the bones it pulls on, and the nerves that fire it lift a backpack together.
look.prompt: Name the level at each zoom step: cell, tissue, organ, system. What is something the biceps can do that a single muscle cell cannot?

check.q: Which of these is a tissue?
choices: A group of muscle cells that shorten together
check.why: A tissue is a group of similar cells doing one job.

check.q: The heart contains muscle tissue, nerve tissue, and connective tissue. What level is the heart?
check.why: An organ is made of several tissues working together on one job.

check.q: Put these in order from smallest to largest.
check.why: Cells make tissues, tissues make organs, organs make systems.

lessons.title: Digestion and Blood Delivery
lessons.mainIdea: The digestive system breaks food into small pieces, and the circulatory system carries them to every cell.
reading: Bite an apple. The piece in your mouth is far too big for any cell to use. The job of the *digestive system* is to break it down into pieces small enough to pass through a cell membrane. Teeth crush it. Saliva starts to break down starch. The stomach churns it with acid. Then the small intestine, a tube about six meters long in an adult, finishes the work with chemicals called enzymes.

The wall of the small intestine is lined with millions of tiny fingers called villi. They soak up the sugars and other small molecules from the broken-down food. From there the food molecules pass into the blood. What the body cannot digest moves on to the large intestine and leaves the body as waste.

Now the *circulatory system* takes over. The heart is a pump made of muscle. It pushes blood through tubes called blood vessels: arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins bring it back, and tiny capillaries connect them. Capillaries are so thin that food molecules and oxygen can pass through their walls to reach cells. An adult heart at rest pumps about 5 liters of blood every minute, roughly the whole body's supply.

So the two systems form a chain. Digestion makes food small enough to enter the blood. Circulation delivers that food to a muscle cell in your toe or a nerve cell in your brain. Neither system could feed a cell alone.

words.d: the organs that break food into molecules small enough for cells to use
the heart, blood, and blood vessels that carry food and oxygen to cells and waste away

look.title: Harvey Follows the Blood
look.text: In 1628 the English doctor William Harvey published a short book arguing that blood moves in a circle. He measured how much blood the heart pushes out with each beat and multiplied by the number of beats. The total was far more than the body could make from food in that time. So, he reasoned, the same blood must go around and come back, again and again.
look.cite: William Harvey, On the Motion of the Heart and Blood in Animals, 1628
look.prompt: Harvey used a calculation, not a microscope, to argue that blood circulates. Why was multiplying beats times blood per beat such strong evidence?

check.q: Why does food need to be digested before cells can use it?
choices: The pieces must be small enough to pass through a cell membrane
Cells cannot use food at all
check.why: Cells can only take in molecules small enough to cross the membrane.

check.q: Which blood vessels are thin enough for food and oxygen to pass through their walls?
check.why: Capillaries have very thin walls so molecules can move between blood and cells.

check.q: What would happen to a muscle cell in your foot if the circulatory system stopped?
choices: It would digest its own food
It would get food from the skin
It would run out of food and oxygen
check.why: Cells depend on blood to deliver food and oxygen. Without circulation they starve.

lessons.title: Breathing In, Breathing Out
lessons.mainIdea: The respiratory system brings oxygen into the blood and removes carbon dioxide from it.
reading: Hold your breath. Within a minute your chest starts to burn and your body demands air. That demand is not really about air. It is about oxygen, which your mitochondria need to release energy, and about carbon dioxide, a waste gas they make that must leave. Moving those two gases is the job of the *respiratory system*.

Air enters through your nose or mouth and travels down the windpipe, or *trachea*, into the lungs. Inside the lungs the tubes branch again and again, like a tree turned upside down, ending in millions of tiny air sacs called *alveoli*. Each alveolus is wrapped in capillaries. Oxygen crosses the thin wall into the blood, and carbon dioxide crosses the other way into the air.

You breathe because of a sheet of muscle under your lungs called the *diaphragm*. When it pulls down, your chest gets bigger and air rushes in. When it relaxes, air flows out. A resting adult breathes about 12 to 20 times a minute. Running makes you breathe faster because your muscle cells are burning fuel faster and need more oxygen.

Here again two systems work as one. The respiratory system loads oxygen into blood in the lungs. The circulatory system carries that blood to every cell. Blood coming back is loaded with carbon dioxide, which the lungs breathe out. Every breath is a delivery and a pickup.

words.d: the lungs and airways that bring oxygen into the blood and remove carbon dioxide
the windpipe, the tube that carries air from the throat to the lungs
tiny air sacs in the lungs where oxygen enters the blood
the sheet of muscle under the lungs that moves to pull air in and push it out

look.title: The Upside-Down Tree
look.text: Imagine your lungs as a tree standing on its head. The trunk is the trachea. It splits into two thick branches, one for each lung. Each branch splits into smaller branches, then twigs, over and over. At the tip of every twig is a cluster of tiny hollow grapes, the alveoli, each wrapped in a net of blood vessels. Spread flat, the inner surface of all those sacs would cover a large room.
look.prompt: Why would lungs with millions of tiny sacs move more oxygen than lungs shaped like two simple balloons of the same size?

check.q: Where does oxygen actually enter the blood?
check.why: Alveoli are the tiny sacs wrapped in capillaries where gases cross into and out of blood.

check.q: What makes air flow into your lungs?
choices: The lungs pull air in with their own muscle
The diaphragm pulls down, making the chest larger
Air is pushed in by the heart
check.why: The diaphragm is the muscle that changes the size of the chest and moves air.

check.q: Why do you breathe faster when you run?
choices: Muscle cells burn fuel faster and need more oxygen
check.why: Working muscles use oxygen faster and make more carbon dioxide, so breathing speeds up.

lessons.title: Muscles and Bones
lessons.mainIdea: The skeletal system gives the body its frame, and the muscular system moves it by pulling on bones.
reading: Stand up and bend your arm. Feel the bump on the front of your upper arm get harder. That is a muscle shortening. Now feel your elbow. That hard knob is bone. Motion is what happens when muscle and bone work together. The *skeletal system* is the frame. The *muscular system* is the engine.

An adult human has about 206 bones. Bones are alive. They are made of cells that lay down hard minerals, mostly calcium, in a tough web. Bones hold you up, protect soft organs like the brain and heart, and store minerals. Inside some bones is marrow, which makes new blood cells. Where two bones meet is a *joint*. Some joints, like the knee, swing like a hinge. Others, like the shoulder, roll in a socket.

Muscles can only pull. They cannot push. So muscles come in pairs. When your biceps on the front of your arm shortens, your arm bends. To straighten it, the biceps relaxes and the triceps on the back pulls. Muscles attach to bones with tough cords called tendons. Every movement, from a blink to a jump, is muscles pulling on bones.

Not all muscle is under your control. The muscle in your heart beats on its own. Muscle in the walls of your stomach and intestines squeezes food along without any thought from you. Only the muscles attached to your skeleton wait for your command.

words.d: the bones that support the body, protect organs, and give muscles something to pull on
the muscles that move the body by pulling on bones or squeezing organs
a place where two bones meet and can move

look.title: Where the Bones Are
look.prompt: Your two hands and two feet together hold more than half of your 206 bones. Why might hands and feet need so many small bones instead of a few big ones?

check.q: Why do muscles work in pairs?
choices: One rests while the other works
One is for the left side and one for the right
Muscles can only pull, not push
check.why: A muscle can only shorten. A second muscle must pull the other way to reverse the motion.

check.q: Which of these is a job of the skeletal system?
check.why: Bones support the body and protect soft organs such as the brain inside the skull.

check.q: What connects a muscle to a bone?
check.why: Tendons are tough cords that attach muscle to bone.

lessons.title: Nerves and Control
lessons.mainIdea: The nervous system senses the world, carries signals, and tells the other systems what to do.
reading: Touch a hot pan and your hand jerks back before you even feel the pain. Something in your body sensed the heat, decided, and moved your arm in a fraction of a second. That something is the *nervous system*: the brain, the spinal cord, and the nerves that reach every part of the body.

The nervous system is built from cells called *neurons*. A neuron has a cell body, short branches that receive signals, and one long fiber that carries a signal away. Signals travel as tiny electrical pulses. When a pulse reaches the end of a neuron, it passes a chemical to the next neuron across a tiny gap. Chains of neurons carry messages from your fingertip to your spinal cord to your brain and back.

The *brain* is the control center. It receives signals from your eyes, ears, skin, nose, and tongue. It compares them to what it remembers. Then it sends commands out. Some jobs, like breathing and heartbeat, the brain runs without your attention. Others, like reaching for a cup, you decide.

The hot-pan jerk is a reflex. The signal goes to the spinal cord and straight back to the arm muscles, skipping the brain, because waiting would mean a worse burn. The pain arrives a moment later, when the message reaches the brain. Your nervous system is fast, but it is also organized to be faster where speed matters most.

words.d: the brain, spinal cord, and nerves that sense, decide, and send commands
nerve cells that carry electrical signals through the body
the organ that receives signals from the senses and controls the body's responses

look.title: One Second at the Stove
look.text: Time zero: a fingertip brushes a hot pan. Heat sensors in the skin fire. The signal races up the arm nerve to the spinal cord. There, a neuron passes it straight to a motor neuron running back down to the arm muscles. The hand snaps away. Only after that does a copy of the signal climb to the brain, and you feel the sting and say ouch.
look.prompt: Why is it useful that the reflex skips the brain? What might go wrong if every action had to wait for the brain?

check.q: What carries signals through the nervous system?
check.why: Neurons are the nerve cells that carry electrical pulses from one place to another.

check.q: In a reflex, where does the signal turn around and head back to the muscle?
check.why: Reflexes are handled in the spinal cord so the response is faster than waiting for the brain.

check.q: Which of these does the brain control without you thinking about it?
check.why: Breathing and heartbeat run automatically. Reaching, choosing, and writing are decisions you make.

lessons.title: One Body, Many Systems
lessons.mainIdea: No body system works alone; each depends on the others to keep every cell alive.
reading: The starting gun fires and a runner leaves the blocks. In the next ten seconds, every system you have read about goes to work at once. Her nervous system hears the gun and fires her leg muscles. Her muscular system pulls on the bones of her skeletal system. Her heart pounds to push more blood, and her lungs gulp air. Her digestive system provided the fuel hours ago.

Take any one system away and the race ends. Without the circulatory system, the oxygen from her lungs could not reach her legs. Without the nervous system, her muscles would not know when to pull. Without bones, her muscles would have nothing to pull on. The systems are linked like the parts of a machine, but they are also linked at the level of cells. Every cell in her leg needs food, oxygen, signals, and a way to dump waste.

That is why the body keeps its inside conditions steady even when the outside changes. Her body temperature climbs as she runs, so she sweats and blood flows near the skin to cool her. Her muscles make more carbon dioxide, so she breathes faster to clear it. Scientists call this steady balance *homeostasis*. It is the work of all the systems together.

So the answer to this chapter's big question is a chain. Trillions of cells become a body because cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form systems, and the systems constantly serve each other. The runner is one organism, but she is also a partnership of every cell in her.

words.d: the way a body keeps its inside conditions, like temperature, steady while the outside changes
a set of parts that work together, in the body a group of organs with one shared goal

look.title: Cold Day at the Bus Stop
look.text: It is a January morning in Chicago, well below freezing. A student waits for the bus. Within minutes she starts to shiver. Her fingers go pale as blood pulls back from the skin toward her core. Her heart rate stays steady. Her breath fogs. She stamps her feet. Twenty minutes later, on the warm bus, the shivering stops and her fingers turn pink again.
look.prompt: Which body systems were involved in keeping her core warm? Why would the body pull blood away from the fingers on purpose?

check.q: Which system delivers the oxygen that the lungs take in to the leg muscles?
check.why: The circulatory system carries oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to every cell.

check.q: What is homeostasis?
choices: The way muscles pull on bones
The way the brain stores memories
Keeping inside conditions steady when the outside changes
check.why: Homeostasis is the body's steady internal balance, such as keeping temperature near normal.

check.q: Why does a runner breathe faster and sweat more during a race?
choices: Her nervous system has shut off
She is digesting a large meal
Her cells are making more carbon dioxide and heat that must be removed
check.why: Hard-working cells produce extra waste gas and heat, and the systems adjust to clear them.

review.q: What did Hooke actually see when he looked at cork in 1665?
choices: The walls of dead plant cells
review.why: Cork is dead bark. Hooke saw the empty cell walls that remained.

review.q: What is the basic unit of life, the smallest thing that is alive on its own?
review.why: The cell theory says the cell is the smallest living unit.

review.q: Which organelle holds the DNA instructions in a plant or animal cell?
review.why: The nucleus contains the cell's DNA.

review.q: A cell under the microscope is green and boxy. What is it most likely?
review.why: Chloroplasts make it green and a cell wall makes it boxy. Only plant cells have both.

review.q: Which is the correct order from smallest to largest?
choices: Cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism
Organ, cell, tissue, organism, organ system
Tissue, organ, cell, organ system, organism
Organism, organ system, organ, tissue, cell
review.why: Cells build tissues, tissues build organs, organs build systems, systems build the organism.

review.q: A person's lungs fill with air but the oxygen cannot reach their leg muscles. Which system is most likely failing?
review.why: The circulatory system carries oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body.

review.q: Why does the body need muscles in pairs, such as the biceps and triceps?
choices: Because a muscle can only pull, not push
review.why: One muscle bends the joint and its partner straightens it, since muscles only shorten.

review.q: You touch a sharp tack and your hand jerks away before you feel pain. What explains the order of events?
choices: The brain is faster than the spinal cord
Muscles can sense pain on their own
The reflex is handled in the spinal cord before the signal reaches the brain
review.why: Reflexes skip the brain for speed. The feeling of pain comes when the signal reaches the brain a moment later.
